item.title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2e074nn8eko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban - Published The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind. "It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan. The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins. "But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags. Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran. They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world. Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021. Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt. The expulsions show no sign of stopping. The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR. "In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan. "We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border. It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go. Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all. "I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry. "We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says. "But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police." Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan. The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law". Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden. The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants". In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025. The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel". The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified". But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in". Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children. Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university? Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried." Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified. "I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house. "We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside." He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work. "I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country. Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights. Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN. But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000. At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face. "There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan." In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide. The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition. "No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive. But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support". Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve. The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule. But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states. As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?" He answers his own question: "Nothing." We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense. All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing. Related topics - Published31 July 2025 - Published24 August

item.title: Nepal death toll crosses 1,000 as rescuers race to find workers trapped in mud-filled tunnels
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ylvgq9q71o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Nepal death toll crosses 1,000 as rescuers race to find workers trapped in mud-filled tunnels - Published The death toll in Nepal from devastating floods on the border with Tibet has crossed 1,000, according to the country's disaster agency. More than 3,900 people remain missing - of whom more than 600 are workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower sites along Trishuli River. Engineers have been pumping air into the tunnels - and while a team did manage to gain entry to one of them, it withdrew after finding no-one there. "I wish we could find him. I wish he would come home," Anushila Bhandari, wife of Aurus Bhandari, a 33-year-old engineer missing on a project site, told BBC Nepali. Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites. The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved. "I still have a 50% hope that he is alive because there is an oxygen system inside," Sita Pandey, whose husband was working in the plant when the floods hit, told Nepalese daily Kantipur. Nepal relies heavily on hydropower and has spent years developing the projects along its mountainous river systems. At least 11 projects either completed or under construction were damaged in the floods, authorities said. Rescuers began pumping air into a tunnel over the weekend, but the families of those trapped say that should have been done earlier. A team was able to get into a tunnel leading to one hydropower plant earlier on Monday, but retreated after no one was found there. "The longer it takes, the more our hope dies. This operation must move much faster because every second is meaningful to us," Jiban Khadka, whose relative is also trapped inside the plant, told Kantipur. "It's a frustratingly slow operation," Khadka added. Rescue operations had been "intensified", Nepalese leader Shah said, noting that the floods were "not an ordinary" event. "This incident indicates that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change. "It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change," Shah wrote in a Facebook post late on Monday. Another family member anxiously awaiting news is Priya Kharel, whose brother Milan was working as an engineer in the Upper Trishuli-1 plant when the floods hit. "Those who returned from the hydropower site said there were people inside the tunnel," she told BBC News Nepali. "So there is hope that if the army reaches them quickly, they can be saved." Australian engineer Arnold Dix, who has been helping Nepalese authorities with the underground search operations remotely, said rescuers had been struggling to find the tunnels. "The actual signature of them has gone – everything is just missing. It looks like a lunar landscape," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One. Once rescuers knew where the power stations were, Dix said they could then decide the best way to access them, which typically involves digging and "blasting boulders". "There's boulders bigger than houses. I've never seen that before in my life. It's just an extraordinary operation," the former head of the International Tunnelling Association said. He said he still has some hope for those trapped underground, given the protection the subterranean environment might have offered from the deluge above. Only 4% of the 900 bodies that have been found so far have been identified, a spokesperson from the Ministry of Health told BBC Nepali. In Chitwan, a district far downstream from where the floods first hit, makeshift burials were taking place after the Himalayan nation's river systems brought nearly 300 dead bodies to its banks. The air was thick with the smell of decay, as men wearing white Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including masks carried unidentified corpses into trucks. Over the weekend, a large portion of the forest outside the city was dug up. Medical staff and volunteers worked to extract DNA from the unidentified remains. Ganesh Aryaal, the chief district officer, told BBC Nepali that relatives will still be able to extricate the remains of their loved ones, once they are identified through DNA testing. "We don't have enough freezers here... We had to choose this last alternative of temporary burial system. We are really overwhelmed," he said. In Tibet, the Chinese-appointed Panchen Lama - who is the second-highest spiritual leader in Tibetan Buddhism - held a memorial service as search teams continued to wade through waist-high mud. The official death toll on the Tibetan side is 16, with 546 reported missing, according to Chinese state media. Footage of the floods has been heavily censored in China. The base of a single water tower is the only structure still standing in the once bustling border crossing with Nepal, state media report. Chinese authorities have imposed "administrative penalties" – which can range from warnings and fines to short detentions – on people speculating online that the casualty numbers are a lot higher than reported. In Nepal, authorities have also ordered the removal of online content that they deem to be misinformation about the floods. Get in touch How have you been affected by the events in Nepal? Let us know. Additional reporting by Jugal Purohit in Chitwan and Binita Dahal, BBC Nepali - Published4 hours ago

item.title: The final minutes before floodwater crashed through Nepal-China border
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qxw1qw3g7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The final minutes before floodwater crashed through Nepal-China border - Published The video lasts only seconds. A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The timestamp on the CCTV footage reads 10:59:53 local time. What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery from before and after the disaster have begun to reveal the scale of the destruction. Much of the border complex appears to have been swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone. Gyirong was one of the places devastated by the floods that tore through the region on 26 August. Just across the frontier, at Rasuwagadhi in Nepal's Rasuwa district, the destruction was also extensive. The Friendship Bridge linking Nepal and China was swept away, along with Nepal's immigration and customs facilities. Timure, the small trading settlement clustered around the crossing, was devastated. "This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet. The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders," says Ajay Dixit, a Kathmandu-based hydrologist. The route remains an important gateway between Nepal and China. It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border. On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry. Nepal's Department of Immigration has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster. Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal. The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 8:35:03am local time (10:52am Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong. Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing. Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy. Tika Ram Pokharel, a senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, was the only member of his office known to have survived. He had travelled to Kathmandu to sit an exam that day. But he says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning. The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing. The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing. When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area. "Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel told the BBC. Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration. Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together. That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck. At 8:37am - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood. China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes. People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear. And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices. It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day. "My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said. Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified. The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away. For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open. Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped. Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area. When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins." The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge. Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult. Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese. Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China. Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour. Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China. Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports. The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network. "Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says. "We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port." Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing. The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck. "But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

item.title: Israeli fire kills three in Gaza City during reported raid, medics say
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1wxex4vg35o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Israeli fire kills three in Gaza City during reported raid, medics say - Published At least two Palestinian children and a woman have been killed by Israeli fire in western Gaza City, Palestinian medics say. Unconfirmed local reports say that an Israel-backed Palestinian militia carried out a raid and that the Israeli military carried out shelling and air strikes after it was discovered. A third child was killed in a separate incident in central Gaza. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said that a senior Hamas official had been arrested, but it is not clear whether the announcement is related to the incident in Gaza City. Videos from Gaza City captured chaotic scenes, with the sound of gunfire and the aftermath of air strikes. Initial Palestinian reports said that a special Israeli unit infiltrated a crowded area using a van and motorcycles. It is not clear whether those involved were Israeli forces or members of an Israel-backed Palestinian militia. A local source told the BBC that a senior Hamas security official was believed to have been targeted. The Israeli military reportedly carried out drone strikes to try to secure the special unit after its presence was uncovered. The military has only confirmed striking several targets in Gaza "in order to remove threats to the security forces", adding that there were no injuries to its troops. item.title: Ex-gang boss guilty of orchestrating 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c24j5192j7jo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ex-gang boss guilty of orchestrating 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur - Published Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been found guilty of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur - the first conviction in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years. The jury found him guilty of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996. Dressed in a black suit, the 63-year-old stood impassively in the Las Vegas court as the verdict was read, before saying he would appeal. During the trial, the court heard a recording of a police interview in 2008 in which Davis said he was in the car from which shots were fired, but did not himself fire the bullets that killed Shakur. Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire. Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur. As the verdict was read out on Monday, Shakur's relatives held hands, some hugging and crying. Shakur was 25 when he was slain at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide. For 30 years, the case remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - but never a conviction, until now. During the trial, prosecutors said Davis had planned the shooting as retaliation after Anderson was involved in a fight with Shakur and his crew in Las Vegas just hours earlier. Shakur's murder happened at a time of intense rivalry between the East Coast and West Coast rap scene and amid gang feuds between the Bloods and Crips, which had deep roots within hip-hop at the time. His family appeared emotional in court, his sister embracing a prosecutor after the verdict was read while others sat crying nearby. Outside, devoted fans of Shakur were similarly crying and cheering. The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, in which he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired. He had told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview related to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace. Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend. But his book and media interviews voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges being filed, with the court ruling his police interview could be used in the murder trial against him. - Tupac murder accused told police in 2008 his nephew fired fatal shots - Published21 August In closing arguments, prosecutor Binu Palal told jurors to take Davis at his word and find him guilty. For years, he argued, Davis had been telling people "that he is responsible for Tupac Shakur's murder" through documentaries, his memoir, podcasts and a police interview. "He's the shot caller - in every instance in every iteration he's the leader of the South Side Crips," Palal told the jury. "When you have the shot caller sitting shotgun when shots are fired, there's no doubt he's responsible." Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money. In closing arguments, his lawyer Michael Sanft urged the jury to discredit his client as a liar who just told tales to sell books. "There's no proof," he told the jury. But within hours of the jury being handed the case on Monday, they reached a guilty verdict. Just before the court emptied out, Clark County District Court Judge Carli Kierny set Davis' sentencing for 13 October. While reading out some procedural steps in the case, Davis appeared to interrupt by raising his hand. "I would like my stuff," he told the judge, mentioning some personal items including his phone. He continued: "I would like to appeal this matter." The judge explained that this could happen after sentencing. Get all the latest trial updates on the BBC Sounds 'Fame Under Fire: The Tupac Murder Trial' podcast available wherever you get your BBC podcasts.

item.title: Teen girl charged with murder over recording of San Diego mosque attack
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2dw3wn972no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Teen girl charged with murder over recording of San Diego mosque attack - Published A 17-year-old girl has been charged with murder by aiding and abetting after prosecutors say she recorded a livestream of an attack on a San Diego mosque that left three people dead. Prosecutors say the girl also published a manifesto from two teenage gunmen who carried out the attack on the Islamic Center of San Diego on 18 May. The teenager, from North Carolina, was arrested last week and indicted by a grand jury on Monday, according to Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O'Neill. Speaking at a news conference, O'Neill said: "The thought of her going back to school, with the weekend approaching, holy days approaching, we didn't know what she was capable of." The teenager now faces three murder charges and one count of conspiracy. O'Neill explained that under North Carolina law, a person accused of aiding and abetting a crime can be held criminally responsible in the same way as the person who carried it out. Authorities say the attack was carried out by two males - aged 17 and 18 - who opened fire at the mosque, before taking their own lives. O'Neill said the pair had two aims that day: "Number one, to kill as many people as possible on that day. Secondly, they wanted this carnage and destruction recorded ... livestreamed." A security guard at the mosque, Amin Abdullah, exchanged gunfire with the attackers and initiated a lockdown, helping protect around 140 children who were inside the building. Abdullah and two worshippers - Mansour Kaziha and Nader Awad, who drew the attentions of the shooters in a parking lot - were fatally shot. San Diego Police Chief Scott Wahl previously described Abdullah's actions as "heroic", saying they had "undoubtedly" saved lives. According to investigators, the shooters recorded the attack using cameras mounted on GoPro-style helmets. O'Neill said the pair had also planned further attacks "at a local Jewish temple and finally at a predominantly African American high school". Authorities said the teenagers had an arsenal of around 30 guns and a crossbow, which investigators say were taken from one of the shooter's parents. The attackers also left behind writings containing racist and antisemitic views, as well as references to white supremacist ideologies. The document, which was reviewed by the BBC's US news partner CBS News, pointed to a gunman who murdered 51 people at two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 2019, as one of their models. item.title: Amazon rigged $20bn worth of ad prices, US lawsuit alleges
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy91nvy27o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Amazon rigged $20bn worth of ad prices, US lawsuit alleges - Published Amazon secretly overcharged more than a million advertising customers by manipulating online auctions it uses to set ad prices, according to a lawsuit filed by the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and a bipartisan group of 22 states. According to the lawsuit, filed on Monday, the alleged scheme has likely netted the firm $20bn (£14.8bn) from advertising customers since 2019. "Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits," says a complaint filed in the company's home state of Washington. In a statement to the BBC, Amazon said it "strongly disagrees" with the premise that it misled advertisers and called the suit "misguided." In addition to advertisers, the FTC, a US consumer watchdog, and the states say Amazon customers have also been harmed as extra costs are passed onto shoppers. "Consumers are suffering, have suffered, and will continue to suffer substantial injury as a result," the complaint states, prompting swift pushback from Amazon. "The FTC wants the public to believe this case is about higher prices for consumers. It is not," Amazon said in its statement. The company's shares fell following the announcement of the lawsuit, closing 2.5% lower on Monday. Many brands and sellers compete on Amazon to place Sponsored Product ads and Sponsored Brands ads when consumer search for products using keywords on Amazon's e-commerce platform. Those placements are then auctioned off to the highest bidder. The complaint accuses Amazon of secretly charging advertisers more in so-called "second price" auctions, whereby prospective advertisers expect to pay one cent more than the next highest bidder for each bid they win. But in practice, the complaint alleges, Amazon has charged its Sponsored Products advertisers their own winning bid close to 80% of the time. The lawsuit states that Amazon's methods were spurred because "it was unhappy about how much revenue its advertising auctions were generating". Amazon responded by saying the FTC "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate". "Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics," Amazon said in its statement. "Average winning bids fell 50% from 2019 to 2025 on Sponsored Products search ads, and roughly 92% of placed ads are not given to the highest bid," the company added. Amazon has tangled with the consumer watchdog in the past. Last year, it settled a case with the FTC that alleged that it enrolled millions of consumers in its Prime subscription offering without their consent, and knowingly made it difficult for consumers to cancel. item.title: Shein valued at $26bn after long-awaited stock market debut
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3v0qrz7z25o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Shein valued at $26bn after long-awaited stock market debut - Published Ultra-fast-fashion brand Shein has been valued at $26.2bn (£19.3bn) after its first day of public trading, following a long quest to list on the stock market. The company was once estimated to be worth nearly $100bn, but has faced heated competition, trade tensions and questions over the ethics of its supply chain. Shein's share price fell in the early hours of trading but recovered ground before closing down just 0.12%. The company's attempts to list in the UK and US were scuppered after supply chain concerns and criticism of its environmental impact. On Monday, Shein priced its shares at HK$48.56 each, raising 13.6 billion Hong Kong dollars ($1.7bn; £1.3bn) from the listing. That gave the company a stock market valuation of $26.3bn. Shein's shares fell by as much as 10% in early trading before the losses eased. They closed at $48.50, leaving it valued at $26.15bn. Shein became hugely popular, especially among younger people, due to its ability to source the very latest fashions at ultra-low prices through a vast network of factories in China. At a ceremony to celebrate the listing, chief financial officer Leigh Gui said the company's model of selling large numbers of small orders with rapid payment options now reaches about 160 markets worldwide. "Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion," he said after a gong was struck to mark the start of trading. Shein has more than 273 million active customers who placed a total of more than a billion orders in the year to the end of March 2026, the firm said in a filing ahead of the listing. But it now faces higher costs, regulatory scrutiny and more competition, said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. For customers, the slump in Shein's shares is a sign that the firm's cheap prices are "becoming harder to sustain", which may lead to higher prices, she added. A benchmark for fast fashion The listing marks the largest new share sale in Hong Kong so far this year, which is being seen as a test of investor appetite for the fast-fashion industry. It is a rare "standalone" e-commerce firm that can be assessed on its own merits, fashion industry analyst Louise Deglise-Favre from research firm GlobalData. Shares in rivals Asos and Boohoo have been battered in recent years as they face regulatory scrutiny and fierce competition. "Investors have learned to be sceptical," while concerns over sustainability and ethical issues add to the complexity of Shein's share sale, Deglise-Favre said. - The rise and rise of fashion giant Shein - Published7 June 2024 - The truth behind your $12 dress: Inside the Chinese factories fuelling Shein's success - Published12 January 2025 Founded in China and headquartered in Singapore since 2021, Shein has spent several years touting its credentials as a global company, but ultimately was forced to return to its Asian roots to go public. The company once looked set for one of the largest stock market debuts ever by a Chinese firm, with Wall Street in its sights. The firm's long road to the stock market highlights the geopolitical pressures and regulatory scrutiny faced by Chinese companies with global ambitions. Its business had surged during the Covid-19 pandemic as people, stuck at home, turned to online retailers. At the same time, social media influencers shared their hauls for millions of followers to see. Shein faced resistance from US lawmakers, who objected to the planned listing over concerns of forced labour in its factories. In response to such allegations, the company has said it takes a "zero-tolerance policy for forced labour". An initial public offering (IPO) in the US - by far Shein's largest market - would have offered it a chance to further increase its global profile and tap into Western financing. It has also been accused of copying other designers' ideas. Shein has said "it takes all claims of infringement seriously" and that it respects the rights of all designers. Shein also explored the possibility of making its stock market debut in London but faced similar opposition. The BBC has contacted Shein for further comment. 'Only realistic path' In 2025, Shein shifted its attention to Hong Kong, with Chinese authorities approving the move in July this year. "Shein ran out of venues that could take it," said Ashley Dudarenok, founder of Chinese market research firm ChoZan. The company attempted to "look less Chinese" by shifting its headquarters to Singapore ahead of its IPO bid, but it never won political backing abroad nor assurances from Beijing, she added. Headwinds ahead Trade tensions and regulatory concerns mean Shein is navigating a very different landscape to when it first started exploring a potential IPO. In July, it reported a $99m quarterly loss as its sales slowed after the US struck down an import duty exemption on small packages. The exemption, known as the de minimis rule, had helped Shein and rival Temu grow rapidly as it allowed packages worth less than $800 to enter the US without incurring import duties. Similarly, the European Union has imposed a €3 (£2.57; $3.50) tax on low-value imports. The Iran war has also hit demand, raised costs and caused delays to deliveries in some markets, Shein has said. Its rivals are feeling the pressure too. In August, Temu-owner PDD reported lower-than-expected quarterly revenue. The company also needs to find ways to stand out from its rivals, that are now also using predictive technology to make their websites more appealing to shoppers, said Jason Hsu from Rayliant Global Advisors. "Shein is not longer a unique player," Hsu said. Shein is also being investigated by US and European regulators over its business practices. item.title: South Korean police officer admits to closing missing person cases to avoid work
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c780wy7ype4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
South Korean police officer admits to closing missing person cases to avoid work - Published A South Korean police officer has admitted to closing missing persons cases without investigating them in order to avoid additional work, according to authorities. The officer, surnamed Bu, was arrested earlier this month after he was accused of prematurely closing cases on the popular holiday island Jeju and lying to missing persons' families. Amid mounting public criticism, police embarked on belated searches for several missing persons on the island, and have since discovered four bodies in recent weeks. The scandal has prompted President Lee Jae Myung to vow to reform the police, as the government prepares to give the police more powers. On Tuesday, the Jeju Provincial Police said Bu had falsely closed at least two high-profile cases and had been charged with forgery of public electronic records, obstruction of official duties and dereliction of duty. In both cases, Bu had falsely claimed he had contacted the missing persons and then prematurely closed their cases without confirming their whereabouts and safety. A police statement said that during their investigations into Bu, he had "stated to the effect that 'the missing person was a typical adult so I thought about it carelessly. If the case was not closed, there would have been a lot to take care of, and out of a sense of pressure over the case handover, I falsely closed it'." One of the cases involved a 37-year-old woman named Jang Mi-ran who went missing in May and was reported missing by her boyfriend. At the time, Bu had told Jang's boyfriend that he had spoken to her and she did not want to meet the police nor be contacted by her boyfriend. Authorities later said that this was a complete fabrication by Bu. Bu had entered this false information into the system, and also logged that Jang had died in a traffic accident, before closing the case, according to authorities. Jang's body was found near a palm tree plantation on Jeju last week. In another case where a man in his 60s was reported missing in July, Bu similarly falsely claimed that he had spoken to the man and that the man did not want to be contacted. The man was eventually found dead earlier this month. Police also said that they believe Bu could have prematurely closed another 25 missing persons cases, though in some of those cases the people were eventually confirmed to be alive and safe. - Bodies found on S Korean holiday island as missing persons scandal deepens - Published6 days ago Violent crime is rare in South Korea, where suicide rates are among the highest in the world. While more than 70,000 adults are reported missing in South Korea each year, 99% of them are marked as resolved within a month. This scandal comes at a politically sensitive time for the country's police. The government had recently passed laws to transfer full investigative power from the prosecutors to the police, a move they said was intended to curtail the prosecutors' influence in politics. However, this move has been unpopular among the public, who have for many years accused the police of corruption and incompetence. President Lee has vowed to reform the police in the wake of recent criticism. On Tuesday President Lee said that it was "regrettable" that because of a few "loach-like figures who muddy the well water", "the honour and pride of the majority of diligent police officers are being damaged".

item.title: Zambia's president sworn in for second term while opponent detained
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62m7vp5895o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Zambia's president sworn in for second term while opponent detained - Published Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema has been sworn in for a second five-year term following a disputed election and the arrest of his main opponent on treason charges. Hichilema - credited with stabilising the economy - swept to victory on 13 August with 60% of the vote, according to official results. Runner-up Brian Mundubile, who received 38%, alleged that the outcome had been tampered with. He was unable to mount a legal challenge to the result as the courts were sealed off last week on the final day a case could be filed. Election observers said that while polling day was largely peaceful, some have raised questions about the vote tallying process. European Union observers said staff in many tallying centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records. It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters. The day after the poll, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of opposition politicians. The authorities accused the opposition of planning an armed insurrection, which they denied. Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, had gone into hiding. They were detained by police last week and charged at the weekend. When Hichilema, 64, came into office in 2021 after a landslide victory, Zambia had recently defaulted on its international debt and had an annual inflation rate of more than 24%. "We inherited a broken-down country… the economy was declining," Hichilema told the BBC in Lusaka before the election. The former businessman negotiated a restructuring of the debt and rebuilt relations with foreign creditors. Inflation has also come down, but prices are still rising and many continue to struggle with the cost of living. Hichilema now wants to build on the foundations he said he laid over the past five years. He was sworn into office on Tuesday amid jubilant scenes, as thousands of supporters gathered to celebrate the inauguration. Presidents from Kenya, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Namibia and Tanzania are among several African leaders attending the inauguration ceremony at the National Heroes Stadium in the capital. Hichilema was sworn in alongside his running mate, Mutale Nalumango. item.title: US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crr451lpl4no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case - Published The celebrity lawyers hired to represent US musician D4vd in his upcoming murder trial have withdrawn from the case. The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, has been appointed a public defender to mount his defence against the charge of murdering Celeste Rivas Hernandez, 14, whose remains were found in September 2025 in a Tesla registered to his address. Burke, 21, pleaded not guilty to the murder charges in a Los Angeles court on Monday. A judge determined last month that he will stand trial for murder. Prosecutors have alleged he stabbed the teen after years of sexual abuse before dismembering her body. A pre-trial hearing is set for 19 October. Lawyers Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter said in a statement to the BBC that the court had granted their request to withdraw from the case and had appointed the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office to represent the singer. The statement said that D4vd "qualified for appointed counsel". "We continue to support David and his defence against these serious charges," they said. "We are grateful that the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office has taken over the representation and that David has a highly capable and committed team of attorneys and investigators behind him." Berk, who led the defence team, has previously represented US actor Mel Gibson and film mogul Harvey Weinstein, as well as singer Britney Spears and actress Lindsay Lohan. Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel said in a statement that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence". "We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said. - US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of 14-year-old - Published28 July Los Angeles County's top prosecutor, Nathan Hochman, said outside the courtroom on Monday that his office was "ready to proceed" with its case against Burke. He also acknowledged that the singer's change in lawyers could delay proceedings, require additional time to review the evidence, or result in the filing of a motion to dismiss the case. His team was ready for "zealous representation" by the defence, he said. Burke had already entered a not guilty plea to charges of first-degree murder, mutilation of human remains and child sexual abuse. He returned to court on Monday to have the charges against him formally read and re-entered the plea. The murder charges include special circumstances linked to financial gain that could make Burke potentially liable for the death sentence. Prosecutors allege Burke killed Hernandez because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career. Evidence read in Los Angeles court during the preliminary hearing showed threats she made against him on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl. "I swear to GOD I will kill u," one expletive-laden text from Hernandez read, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," the text went on. The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up. Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived.

item.title: US army secretary resigns after months of tension
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czjz31dk1xmo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US army secretary resigns after months of tension - Published US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation after about 18 months in the role. His departure was confirmed by CBS, the BBC's US media partner, which reported it came after months of conflict between him and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. The youngest-ever army secretary has often been referred to as President Donald Trump's "drone guy". Driscoll, 41, has been "highly effective" in advancing Trump's agenda "to Make America Strong Again" and provided "outstanding leadership" during military operations, the White House said in a statement given to CBS. The BBC has contacted the White House, Pentagon and Army for comment. Driscoll is the latest in a string of recent high-profile military leaders to depart, including Navy Secretary John Phelan who abruptly quit in April. Other notable departures include Army Chief of Staff Randy George, Army Gen David Hodne and Maj Gen William Green. Since entering the Pentagon, Hegseth has fired more than a dozen senior military officers, including the chief of naval operations and the Air Force's vice-chief of staff. The details of the behind-the-scenes friction between Driscoll and Hegseth are unclear but CBS notes that the army secretary is good friends with George, who was reportedly asked by Hegseth to resign. The post of army secretary is the top civilian leader of the US Army, directing active duty troops, along with the National Guard and reserve soldiers. Driscoll previously served in the Army and was an officer in 2007 before leading a cavalry platoon and deploying to Iraq for several months in 2009. As army secretary, Driscoll became known as Trump's "drone guy" due to his embrace of emerging battlefield technologies. He took on a leading role last year in talks aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, taking on foreign trips and meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. He's also a close ally and friend of Vice-President JD Vance, whom he met at Yale Law School. During his tenure as head of the US Army, he was a key figure in Trump's deployment of the National Guard to US cities. He also took over the role of acting director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Related topics - Published25 November 2025 - Published23 April

item.title: 'She slipped out of my hand' - children missing after ferry sinks off northern Cyprus
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1mv5ggg1l8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'She slipped out of my hand' - children missing after ferry sinks off northern Cyprus - Published Ayten Bicer felt her 12-year-old daughter slip from her grasp and disappear as the ferry they were travelling on capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, killing eight people. Her daughter Miray and six-year-old son Memhet Asaf are among 20 people still missing after the vessel sunk while en route to Turkey from the coastal town of Kyrenia, in the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus. She and her husband Hayri survived, and like many other families are waiting for news of their loved ones back in port as rescuers continue to search. "She was saying, 'Don't let go'. And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go," Bicer told reporters through tears. Bicer said a suitcase fell on top of her, which forced her daughter from her grip. She managed to grab hold of her daughter's foot, but her shoes were coated in engine oil from the overturned vessel and she slipped through her hands. "It was slippery everywhere. It was like oil. She slipped out of my hand," she recalled. The family was returning to Turkey after a holiday on the Mediterranean island. "We couldn't intervene, we lost our children," Hayri Bicer said. "Two of my three children are gone. We left them. We are leaving them on this island as we go." The vessel had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members. Nineteen passengers are currently being treated in hospitals in northern Cyprus, local authorities say. The eight crew members, including the ship's captain, and one other man were formally arrested on Monday. They will be detained for three days, while warrants have been issued for several other people. The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 (09:30 GMT), en route to the town of Tasucu in Turkey. It had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday but its journey was delayed due to severe storms hitting the island. The seas were still rough on Sunday. Some eyewitness accounts say the double-hulled ferry jolted violently before slamming onto the sea surface, with part of its bow bursting open on impact. Ünal Üstel, prime minister of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized. While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he said. The boat has completely sunk and is lying at a depth of 514m (1,686ft), officials say. Debris remains scattered across the water, including a black wheelie suitcase bobbing on the surface and a sheet of steel that appeared to have broken away from the ferry. Authorities are attempting to recover the vessel's black box recorder to establish what happened. A ship will be arriving from Turkey on Tuesday to help with search efforts, TRNC President Tufan Erhurman said. Meanwhile, a three-day period of national mourning began on Monday. The ferry - a high-speed 40m long, 10m wide Filo Jet vessel - sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic. Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic accident". The TRNC controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974. - Published1 day ago

item.title: US Supreme Court clears way for Trump to keep building White House ballroom
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9w457e7ydlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Supreme Court clears way for Trump to keep building White House ballroom - Published The US Supreme Court has ruled that construction of a $400m (£297m) ballroom at the White House can go ahead, in a victory for President Donald Trump. In a 5-4 ruling, the justices granted the Trump administration's emergency request, blocking lower court rulings that would have halted construction of an above-ground portion of the project. But Chief Justice John Roberts, a conservative, sided with the three liberal justices to dissent, writing that "construction is likely unlawful" because Congress has not approved the project. The National Trust for Historic Preservation filed the legal challenge, arguing that the president did not have unilateral authority to proceed with construction. Trump demolished the historic East Wing of the executive residence last autumn to begin building the ballroom. The White House has said the project will be "substantially" finished by November and fully completed by August 2028. On Friday, the high court had temporarily allowed construction of the 90,000 sq ft (8,400 sq m) ballroom to move forward while the justices considered the lawsuit aiming to halt it entirely. In Monday's unsigned order, the five justices who cleared the way for construction said lower courts had "likely exceeded" their authority in blocking the ballroom. While the majority did not decide on the legality of the East Wing project, they said the preservation group "lacks standing" to sue the government. They ruled that the Trump administration had established it was likely to succeed in arguing that it would "suffer irreparable harm without a stay". Chief Justice Roberts wrote in dissent: "Today's decision is no victory for the separation of powers." Reacting to the ruling, Trump posted that he was "pleased" the "baseless" lawsuit had failed to halt construction. "We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, DC," he said. Trump has long argued that the White House needs a larger events space, and more recently, that it was important for his security. The Republican president emphasised the need for the ballroom after an alleged assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in April. But the National Trust for Historic Preservation argued that construction was causing irreversible damage to a historical landmark. Its position stemmed from a declaration made by preservationist Alison Hoagland, who lives in Washington DC and serves on the trust's board of trustees. Hoagland, who says she visits the neighbourhood once a month, asserted that she would "suffer both professional and personal injuries, including to my aesthetic, cultural and historical interests, if a ballroom of the proposed form and scale were constructed". In the dissent, Roberts said the injuries claimed by Hoagland were sufficient to allow the lawsuit to go ahead. The National Trust for Historic Preservation said it was disappointed in the court's decision, but welcomed the "strong dissent" by Roberts. "Each President is a temporary steward of the People's House and does not have the unilateral authority to demolish and redesign it without the approval of Congress," it said in a statement. The ballroom project, along with the helipad being constructed on the South Lawn, are just part of the president's wider effort to transform Washington's cityscape. His plans include the renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and a planned "Arc de Trump" larger than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

item.title: Festival honouring Dolly Parton set for Nashville and London
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ywd9q3ywvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Festival honouring Dolly Parton set for Nashville and London - Published Dolly Parton's estate has announced a festival honouring the life and legacy of the late singer, set for London and Nashville. The "star-studded" two-day DollyFest will happen across two consecutive weekends in both cities in 2027, her estate said in a Monday press release, adding that the specific dates will be announced later. Parton herself dreamed up an earlier version of the event, where she would host and perform alongside other artists, but the original January 2026 event was called off before it was announced publicly, due to Parton's health struggles, her estate said. "DOLLYFEST will be the party of a lifetime she wanted to share with the world," her estate said. DollyFest will take the place of a traditional public memorial for the artist, who died at the age of 80 on 25 August after a brief battle with cancer. She was laid to rest at a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday, and placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city, her great-niece said. DollyFest organiser Danny Nozell, the founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises, said the estate is not discouraging people from celebrating Dolly in whatever ways they choose, but Parton did not want a traditional memorial. "It feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly," Nozell said. "This is something that is authentic to her, something that feels right to me, and something that artists and fans around the world can participate in, while also giving everyone time to grieve, and giving everyone time to plan." Originally from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, Parton was a country music icon, philanthropist and businesswoman whose most famous songs included Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You. In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote thousands of songs. Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy." Since her death, emotional tributes from celebrities, politicians, and countless fans have flooded social media. "A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, DOLLYFEST is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!)," Nozell said. item.title: Man arrested after Swiss rave shooting that killed woman
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddv92n194vo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Man arrested after Swiss rave shooting that killed woman - Published A 43-year-old Swiss man has been arrested following a shooting at a rave in Switzerland in which a woman was killed. Italian 22-year-old Maria Spinelli was killed and several others injured at a techno rave being held at a horse racing track in Aarau, a town about 46km (29 miles) west of Zurich on Sunday. The shooting initiated a nearly 24-hour manhunt before Aarau cantonal police confirmed they apprehended the suspect shortly before 01:00 local time on Monday (23:00 GMT on Sunday). "The investigation into the exact sequence of events, the background and the possible motive is currently under way," police said in a statement. "At this time, it is assumed that the perpetrator acted alone." Police first received a report of shots fired at the Schachen race track at about 02:30 local time on Sunday. Spinelli died at the scene, while four men and a woman, aged between 24 and 27, were taken to hospital with injuries "ranging from minor to severe". An eyewitness told Swiss news outlet Blick that he had "suddenly heard the gunshots" minutes after the music stopped, initially believing they were fireworks. He said he was told to hide by a man and a woman, the latter of whom was shot. Organisers had expected 3,500 people to attend. Aarau, home to approximately 23,000 people, is less than 40km from the border with Germany, where local media reported police were supporting Swiss forces. The arrest marks a quick progression in the police investigation - on Sunday afternoon, the force in Aarau said it had no leads on the perpetrator and was unsure whether it was one person or several. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni previously said she was confident Swiss authorities would "shed full light on what happened and find anyone responsible". Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement that it was sending officials to Zurich "to closely follow the investigation". Switzerland has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Europe, although violent shootings are rare and tighter controls were introduced in recent years. The last major shooting occurred in 2001, when 14 members of the parliament and local government of Zug, near Lucerne, were killed by a gunman who then took his own life. item.title: US and Iran trade strikes for first time in weeks
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z72x5z1po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US and Iran trade strikes for first time in weeks - Published Iran and the US have traded strikes after American forces attacked two rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The first known US strikes on Iran since late July killed two people and injured two others, according to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which vowed "response and punishment". US Central Command (Centcom) said it took "limited, precise action" after observing Iran preparing to "launch rockets and deploy sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz", according to its spokesperson. Iran said it had struck US military bases in Jordan in response, with Jordan's army saying it had intercepted eight missiles early on Monday morning. Iran's state TV also said the Iranian army had targeted an air base in the UAE with drones. However, the UAE's Ministry of Defence denied the reports that Al-Minhad Air Base had been targeted as "unfounded". The UAE did confirm it shot down a drone. The US strike is the first known attack on Iran since President Donald Trump paused a renewed military campaign in late July. Larak Island is just offshore from the key port of Bandar Abbas and sits right on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global shipping. Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel through before the war began. Since the conflict began in February, the strait has effectively been closed, causing wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets. Iran is currently demanding that tanker traffic pass by Larak Island for checks and reportedly forcing vessels to pay $2m (£1.5m) to cross. Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, said earlier that the attack on Larak was carried out by drones. Hours later, Iranian media carried a statement by the IRGC saying it had attacked the US bases of King Hussein and al-Azraq in Jordan with ballistic missiles in response to the Larak Island attack. Iran's foreign ministry said on Monday it "strongly condemned the American military aggression on Larak", saying the strikes on bases in Jordan were a "legitimate defence". Trump later told Fox News the US would "hit them hard" in response. Later on Monday, Centcom denied an earlier IRGC claim that a supertanker had struck sea mines and caught fire while trying to navigate the Strait of Hormuz via a route not authorised by Iran. Tasnim published a photo appearing to show a vessel on fire, but did not identify the tanker or provide further details, including when the image was taken. The BBC was unable to verify the claimed attack. "This is yet another IRGC attempt to intimidate regional commercial shipping through disinformation," Centcom said. Meanwhile Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a statement quoted by state TV: "We are not seeking war, but we will deliver a decisive response to the aggressors." Hours after the US strike, Trump posted apparent AI videos on Truth Social showing oil infrastructure exploding. One was captioned "Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!!" in reference to a major oil terminal off the coast of Iran which Trump has threatened to take. His post did not elaborate. - Why is the Strait of Hormuz so important? - Published14 July The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to marine traffic. The strait is a narrow stretch of water between Iran, the UAE and Oman that is about 21 miles (33km) at its tightest point. United Nations rules allow countries to exercise control of territorial seas up to 12 nautical miles (13.8 miles) from their coastline. At the narrowest point, the Strait of Hormuz and its shipping lanes lie entirely within Iran and Oman's territorial waters. Iran has fired against vessels it says have sought to cross without its permission. Trump said last week that all mines placed in the Strait of Hormuz by Iran as part of its efforts to blockade the route had been detonated or removed. He said Iran had been warned that any ship or boat deploying new mines would be destroyed. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi described Trump's claim as a "propaganda" deception. Iran is facing renewed economic pressure after Washington announced a fresh sanctions campaign on 24 August aimed at further isolating Tehran and expanding secondary sanctions against its allies. Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the campaign as a continuation of previous US economic measures, which they argue followed Washington's military failure in the recent conflict. The US is also continuing a naval blockade of Iran, which has affected Iran's ability to export oil. item.title: Ex-congressman George Santos banned from betting platform for life
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpwlxy49225o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ex-congressman George Santos banned from betting platform for life - Published Prediction-market operator Kalshi has permanently barred former US congressman George Santos from trading on its platform. The company alleged that Santos, who was expelled from Congress following a series of fraud and identity-theft charges, placed bets in February related to his own attendance at US President Donald Trump's State of the Union address, according to a notice of disciplinary action. Kalshi said its compliance team concluded his activity showed signs of insider dealing, prompting the lifetime ban. It said it was acting independently without waiting for external enforcement action. Santos on X thanked Kalshi for the ban and said "Let's see how much longer you guys are around for". The BBC has contacted Santos for comment. In 2025, Trump ordered the release of Santos, who had been sentenced to a seven-year prison term for wire fraud and identity theft. He had served three months. In July, Santos agreed to pay $35,000 to settle a federal investigation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission into his State of the Union trades. Kalshi, alleging Santos used non-public information to place bets, issued a penalty of $71,356 (£38,000). The disciplinary moves come at a moment when prediction markets – which allow users to wager on outcomes ranging from elections to economic indicators – are facing heightened scrutiny. Both Kalshi and rival Polymarket have reported an uptick in unusual trading patterns, forcing platforms to strengthen monitoring systems and respond more aggressively to potential misconduct. Kalshi said Santos's case was referred to federal authorities earlier this summer after internal systems flagged suspicious behaviour linked to his account. The company said the case centered on his trades in a market tied to whether he would attend Trump's address – an event he could directly influence. Its compliance team found he placed a series of sizeable bets between 2 and 25 February, some of which were based on false or misleading public statements about his plans, according to the company. His comments moved contract prices, and he ultimately earned $17,839.57 from the trades. Santos has denied wrongdoing in various matters but has admitted to stealing identities of nearly a dozen people, including next of kin. He pleaded guilty to wire fraud and aggravated identity theft and served three months in prison before Trump commuted his sentence last year. He embellished much about his biography in the run-up to his election to Congress in 2022. The former lawmaker was only the sixth in US history to be expelled from Congress. The Kalshi episode underscores the growing compliance burden facing prediction markets as they attract more users and move closer to mainstream products. Regulators have signalled that platforms will be expected to meet higher standards as the industry matures, particularly when political or economic events are involved.
